title: Problem Statement and References
content: Erdos posed this problem at Oberwolfach in 1986. Given the partition function $p(n)$ (counting unordered sums of positive integers), define $F(n) = \omega(\prod_{k=1}^n p(k))$ where $\omega(m)$ counts distinct prime factors. Question 1 (Does $F(n) \to \infty$?) was proved by Schinzel via Tijdeman's 1973 result. Question 2 ($F(n) > n$ eventually?) remains open. References include Tijdeman (1973), Schinzel-Wirsing (1987), Erdos-Ivic (1990), and Ono (2000).

title: Partition Function p(n)
content: Defines $p(n) = |\{\text{Nat.Partition}\;n\}|$ using Lean's `Fintype.card`. A partition of $n$ is a multiset of positive integers summing to $n$. The first values are $p(0)=1, p(1)=1, p(2)=2, p(3)=3, p(4)=5, p(5)=7$, verified by `native_decide`. The generating function is $\sum_{n=0}^\infty p(n)q^n = \prod_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{1-q^k}$.

title: Partition Product
content: Defines the cumulative product $\prod_{k=1}^{n} p(k)$ using `Finset.prod` over `Icc 1 n`. Positivity follows from $p(k) \ge 1$ for all $k$. By the Hardy-Ramanujan formula, $\log \prod_{k=1}^n p(k) \sim \pi\sum_{k=1}^n \sqrt{2k/3} \sim \frac{2\pi}{3}\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\, n^{3/2}$, so the product grows super-exponentially.

title: Function F(n): Distinct Prime Factor Count
content: Defines $F(n) = \omega(\prod_{k=1}^n p(k))$ as the cardinality of the `primeFactors` finset of the partition product. The monotonicity claim $F(m) \le F(n)$ for $m \le n$ has a `sorry` — it requires showing that $\text{primeFactors}(a \cdot b) \supseteq \text{primeFactors}(a)$ for positive $a, b$.

title: Schinzel-Wirsing Lower Bound (1987)
content: Schinzel and Wirsing proved $F(n) \gg \log n$, i.e., $\exists c > 0$ such that $F(n) \ge c \log n$ for large $n$. This is the best known unconditional lower bound. The proof analyzes the prime factorization structure of the partition product using multiplicative number theory. The gap between $\log n$ and the conjectured $n$ is enormous.
mathContext: $\exists c > 0,\; F(n) \ge c \log n$ for $n$ sufficiently large

title: Hardy-Ramanujan Asymptotic Formula (1918)
content: The celebrated Hardy-Ramanujan formula gives $p(n) \sim \frac{1}{4n\sqrt{3}} \exp\!\left(\pi\sqrt{\frac{2n}{3}}\right)$. This was the first major application of the circle method in analytic number theory. The exponential growth of $p(n)$ is the key driver: it forces the partition product to have super-exponential growth, which in turn forces new prime factors to appear.

title: Ono's Prime Divisibility Theorem (2000)
content: Ken Ono proved that every prime $p$ divides $p(n)$ for some $n \ge 1$, and in fact for a positive proportion of $n$. The proof uses the theory of modular forms and Galois representations, building on Ramanujan's congruences $p(5n+4) \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$, $p(7n+5) \equiv 0 \pmod{7}$, $p(11n+6) \equiv 0 \pmod{11}$.

title: Part 1: F(n) → ∞ (PROVED)
content: The first part of Erdos's question is resolved: $F(n) \to \infty$. Schinzel observed this follows from combining Hardy-Ramanujan's exponential growth $p(n) \sim ce^{\alpha\sqrt{n}}$ with Tijdeman's 1973 theorem: any sequence of integers growing at least exponentially must accumulate infinitely many distinct prime factors. Full details appear in Erdos-Ivic (1990), page 69.

title: Part 2: F(n) > n Eventually (OPEN CONJECTURE)
content: The conjecture $F(n) > n$ for large $n$ remains open. This asks whether the partition product has 'more primes than its length' — a strong statement about the density of prime factors. The heuristic: by Hardy-Ramanujan, $\log(\prod_{k=1}^n p(k)) \approx cn^{3/2}$, and a typical number of size $N$ has $\sim \log N / \log \log N$ prime factors, giving $F(n) \approx cn^{3/2}/\log n \gg n$. But making this rigorous is hard.
mathContext: $\forall^\infty n,\; F(n) > n$ (OPEN; best known: $F(n) \gg \log n$)

title: F(5) = 4
content: $\prod_{k=1}^5 p(k) = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 = 210 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$. So $F(5) = 4$. Notably, this product is $210 = \binom{10}{4}$, a primorial. Proved by `native_decide` (kernel-level computation).

title: Small Values F(1) through F(4)
content: $F(1) = 0$ ($p(1) = 1$ has no prime factors), $F(2) = 1$ (product $= 2$), $F(3) = 2$ (product $= 6 = 2 \cdot 3$), $F(4) = 3$ (product $= 30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$). Each new partition number $p(k)$ can introduce new primes, but not always: $p(6) = 11$ is prime (adding one new factor), while $p(7) = 15 = 3 \cdot 5$ introduces no new primes.

title: OEIS Sequences A194259 and A194260
content: The partition products form OEIS A194259: $1, 2, 6, 30, 210, 2310, 32340, 614460, \ldots$ The prime factor counts form A194260: $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, \ldots$ Note that $F(6) = F(7) = 5$ because $p(6) = 11$ (new prime) and $p(7) = 15 = 3 \cdot 5$ (no new primes). These sequences provide empirical evidence for the conjecture $F(n) > n$.
